title: Why Picking Your Battles Is A Poor Strategy
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin pushes back against the popular advice to 'pick your battles' with difficult students, arguing it prevents teachers from ever turning around challenging behavior. He lists a series of harms caused by selective enforcement: it breeds resentment and perceived favoritism, erodes trust, invites confrontation and arguing, and unnerves students who can't predict when a rule will actually be enforced. He notes that the very framing of 'battles' implies confrontation—lecturing, scolding, or questioning—which is inherently personal and damaging to the student-teacher relationship. His alternative is a consistently followed classroom management plan that removes the need to selectively engage at all, letting the plan itself 'do the heavy lifting.'
points: Picking your battles means inconsistently responding to misbehavior, which students perceive as unfair favoritism and breeds resentment.
Inconsistent enforcement erodes trust, which is essential to likability, respect, and classroom management influence.
The 'battle' framing implies confrontation—lecturing, scolding, or questioning—which is inherently personal and provokes arguing and pushback.
Difficult students, especially those already 'battle weary,' will argue even at gentle correction once inconsistency sets in.
The alternative is a consistently followed classroom management plan that removes the need to selectively engage at all.
quotes: Picking your battles will prevent you from ever turning around difficult students or creating the well-behaved classroom you really want.
Choosing to respond to misbehavior sometimes and not others breeds resentment—because it’s unfair and students know it.
Whenever you fail to follow your classroom management plan as promised, your integrity takes a hit.
When teachers speak of picking their battles, they're referring to having a confrontation. In other words, they intend to lecture, scold, question, or otherwise persuade students into compliance.
With confrontation and inconsistency equal parts of the toxic brew, picking your battles is like shooting yourself in the foot and pulling the rug out from under yourself at the same time.
For there is no need, not with a well-taught classroom management plan to do the heavy lifting for you.
